query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting a portion of Mo with additional Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will reduce the electronegativity difference and improve dislocation mobility, thereby enhancing room-temperature plasticity without sacrificing high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo with a disordered BCC structure, exhibiting a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but reduced plasticity attributed to high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content by partially replacing it with an extra amount of Nb (e.g., modifying the composition so that a fraction of Mo is substituted by Nb while keeping overall concentrations balanced).
generation.conditions: The intervention is to be performed on samples processed to obtain a single-phase disordered BCC structure and tested under room-temperature compressive loading conditions. The substitution level should remain modest (e.g., below 30% replacement of Mo) to avoid compromising solid-solution strengthening.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform elemental distribution with a reduced electronegativity difference in the alloy lattice, while preserving the disordered BCC phase.
generation.mechanism: By lowering the Mo content and increasing the Nb proportion, the alloy’s overall electronegativity difference is reduced. This diminishes overly directional bonding, thereby enhancing dislocation mobility and plastic deformation mechanisms, while the solid-solution strengthening effect is maintained by Nb.
generation.predicted_outcome: The revised alloy is expected to exhibit improved compressive plasticity (i.e. higher compressive strain) at room temperature while maintaining a yield strength close to the original 1719 MPa, thereby achieving a better strength–plasticity balance.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with 1719 MPa room-temperature compressive yield strength and limited plasticity.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated only if the level of Mo substitution remains modest (e.g., less than 30%) and the single-phase disordered BCC microstructure is preserved; at elevated substitution levels or if secondary phases form, both strength and plasticity may be adversely affected.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal fraction of Mo to be replaced by Nb and the exact improvement in ductility remain uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of alloys with a fixed base composition of NbZrTiHfMo in which varying fractions (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30%) of Mo are substituted by additional Nb. Process all samples to achieve a disordered BCC microstructure and perform room-temperature compressive tests.
measurements: Phase and microstructure verification via XRD and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in compressive plastic strain (improvement beyond baseline) while maintaining yield strength within ±5% of 1719 MPa, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The yield strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was higher in comparison to that of typical RHEAs. When compared to some of the most widely used Ni-based superalloys, the tensile strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was about 400 MPa higher than that of Haynes 230 and a little bit lower than Inconel 618 at the temperature range of RT-1073 K [Figure 5a]. Moreover, when the deformation temperature exceeded 1073 K, the strength of almost all metals and alloys dropped. This was due to the diffusion-controlled deformation mechanism activating above 0.5 to 0.6 Tm and softening the materials as a result []. Therefore, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA not only had a high melting point but also had a high strength without any complicated treatment, which means that it has good prospects for high-temperature applications.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. The TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs prepared by a P/M method exhibited high specific strength and reasonable plasticity both at room temperature and high temperature. The high yield strength of the RHEAs may have come from the uniform microstructure and the solid solution strengthening effect, while the reasonable plasticity may have resulted from the ductile TaNbVTi matrix, which has similar BCC microstructure. The yield strength and compressive strength of the TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs first increased and then decreased with the increase of Al content. Compression plasticity was decreasing. The Al0.2 RHEA had the highest yield strength and compressive strength. According to the traditional theory of solution strengthening [], the yield strength should increase with the increase of Al content, but the actual situation was different. This shows that the traditional solid solution strengthening theory cannot fully explain the relationship between strength and solute Al. Moreover, Al atoms formed covalent bonds with other alloy atoms, which made the strengthening method more complex.
